sections.title: Mishnah: Kesef, Shtar or Bi'ah In; Get or Death Out; the Yevamah
sections.gist: The three ways a woman enters *kiddushin* (betrothal), *kesef* (money), *shtar* (a document) and *bi'ah* (intercourse), with a dispute over the minimum *kesef*; the two ways she leaves; and the parallel rules for a *yevamah*.

bullets.text: Kiddushin is the last tractate of Nashim: four chapters over eighty dapim. Besides *kiddushin* it covers parents and children, agency, conditions and lineage.

The first chapter, forty dapim and the longest in Shas, is about *kinyan* (acquisition) in general: a woman, a *yevamah*, an *eved ivri*, an *eved kena'ani*, land and movables. Each Mishnah names what is acquired and lists how.

children.title: Kesef, Shtar, Bi'ah: Acts of Kiddushin, Not of Nisu'in
children.gist: What each of the three ways involves, and why *kiddushin* must be kept apart from *nisu'in* (full marriage), the later stage of living together.

bullets.text: Mishnah: a woman is acquired in three ways and acquires herself in two. She is acquired through *kesef*, *shtar* and *bi'ah*.

Rashi: "*ve'konah et atzmah*" means she becomes her own, free to marry another man. That is the core of what *kiddushin* does: it binds her so that she may not marry or have relations with anyone else.
*Kesef*: he gives something of value and says "*harei at mekudeshet li*". Witnesses are required, not only as proof but to make the act legally effective, as with a *get*.
The ring is not mentioned in the Bavli or the Yerushalmi. It first appears in the Geonic *Sefer ha'Chilukim*, which records that Eretz Yisrael used a ring and the East did not.
*Shtar*: a paper saying "*harei at mekudeshet li*", given before witnesses. It is fully valid, but there is no sign it was ever used: the Gemara has many stories of *kesef*, none of a *shtar*.

It is a mistake to equate *kesef*, *shtar* and *bi'ah* with the ring, the *ketubah* and the *yichud* room: the *ketubah* and *yichud* belong to *nisu'in*. Some Genizah *ketubot* do contain "*harei at mekudeshet li*", suggesting some communities blurred the two.
*Bi'ah*: a single act done with intent to create *kiddushin*, unlike the ongoing relationship of *nisu'in*.

*Kiddushin* makes her a married woman: another man's *kiddushin* has no effect, relations with another man are adultery, and she needs a *get* to leave. *Nisu'in* (the *chuppah*, treated in Ketubot) begins the shared household and its obligations, such as the husband's support and her earnings going to him.

The two stages served arranged marriages: *kiddushin* bound the parties, even when the girl was a minor betrothed by her father, while *nisu'in* might follow years later. Later practice used *tena'im* with financial penalties for that purpose.
This explains Rashi's precision: he does not mention vows or earnings, because those flow from *nisu'in*. *Kiddushin* alone only forbids her to other men.

children.title: Kesef: A Dinar or a Perutah, and From Mohar to Symbol
children.gist: Beit Shammai require a *dinar* and Beit Hillel a *perutah*; the shiur reads the dispute as the point where *kesef* became symbolic.

bullets.text: Beit Shammai: a *dinar* or anything worth a *dinar*. Beit Hillel: a *perutah* (a small copper coin) or anything worth a *perutah*.
How much is a *perutah*? One-eighth of an Italian *issar*.
"Or its equivalent" means the *kesef* need not be a coin at all. Beit Hillel's copper *perutah* shows that *kesef* here no longer means silver, only something of minimal value.

The Mishnah is layered: a terse core (*kesef*, *shtar*, *bi'ah*), the schools' gloss on what *kesef* means, and the *perutah* definition as a gloss on the gloss. Pegging it to the Italian *issar* suggests several kinds of *issar* circulated.

Read without the gloss, *kesef* would suggest a real price, like the Torah's *mohar* of fifty silver pieces. That sum moved into the *ketubah* as a deferred debt, protecting the wife and slowing divorce. With nothing substantial paid up front, the schools had to ask what *kesef* now means.
Contrast land, acquired later in the chapter through *kesef*, *shtar* or *chazakah*: there *kesef* is the market price, and no one thinks a *perutah* buys a house.

children.title: Leaving: Get or Death; the Yevamah: Bi'ah In, Chalitzah or Death Out
children.gist: A woman acquires herself through a *get* or her husband's death; a *yevamah* is acquired only through *bi'ah* and freed through *chalitzah* or the *yavam*'s death.

bullets.text: A woman acquires herself through a *get* or through her husband's death.
A *yevamah* (a widow whose husband died childless) is acquired by the *yavam* (his brother) only through *bi'ah*.
She acquires herself through *chalitzah* or through the *yavam*'s death.

sections.title: Why 'Nikneit'? Kinyan for Kesef, Then Kiddushin Like Hekdesh
sections.gist: Why this Mishnah alone speaks of *kinyan*: it teaches *kesef*, learned from Efron's field; and it opens in the Torah's language before turning to the Sages', who call it *kiddushin* after *hekdesh* (consecrated property).

children.title: Kesef From Efron's Field: The Gezerah Shavah of Kichah
children.gist: *Kesef* is learned by *gezerah shavah* (verbal analogy) from Avraham's purchase of Efron's field, which the Torah calls a *kinyan*; Tosafot probe the analogy, and the shiur notes that biblical *kichah* means *nisu'in*.

bullets.text: Question: why does this Mishnah say "*ha'ishah nikneit*" (a woman is acquired) while the next chapter says "*ha'ish mekadesh*" (a man betroths)?
Answer: because it wants to teach *kesef*, the standard means of *kinyan*.

*Kesef* in *kiddushin* is learned through a *gezerah shavah* of *kichah* (taking): "*ki yikach ish ishah*" (Devarim 24:1) and, of Efron's field, "I give the money for the field, *kach mimeni*" (Bereshit 23:13). As the field was acquired with *kesef*, so is a woman.

The taking of the field is called *kinyan*: "the field which Avraham acquired" (Bereshit 25:10), or alternatively "*sadot ba'kesef yiknu*" (Yirmeyahu 32:44). So a Mishnah teaching *kesef* says "*nikneit*".

Tosafot: one might think the money was only the price and the field was acquired by another act, such as *chazakah*. "*Sadot ba'kesef yiknu*" shows the giving of *kesef* is itself the act of *kinyan*.

Tosafot ask why Efron's field is needed if *kesef* is already known. Their answer: *kesef* alone need not mean *kinyan*; the *gezerah shavah* makes the *kesef* of *kiddushin* a *kinyan* in the same sense as buying a field.
Tosafot also note the analogy is imperfect: in Avraham's words "*kach mimeni*" the thing taken is the money, while in "*ki yikach ish ishah*" the thing taken is the woman.

In the Torah, *kichah* of a woman means *nisu'in*: "*ve'ish asher yikach et achoto*" is intercourse, and "*ki yikach ish ishah u'va eleha*" is taking her into the household. The Torah's word for *erusin* is *eras*: "who has betrothed a woman (*eras*) and not taken her (*lekachah*)".

So Chazal learn *kiddushin* from verses that, read plainly, speak of *nisu'in*. The Torah's *kinyan* model comes less from the word *kichah* than from *erusin* being made by a *mohar* paid to the father.

children.title: Lishna de'Oraita, Lishna de'Rabbanan: Kiddushin Makes Her Like Hekdesh
children.gist: The Mishnah opens in the Torah's language of *kinyan* and continues in the Sages' language of *kiddushin*, so called because he forbids her to all like *hekdesh*; the shiur sets the *kinyan* model of marriage against the *kiddushin* model.

bullets.text: Question: then let the next chapter also say "*ha'ish koneh*".
Answer: at first the Mishnah uses *lishna de'Oraita*, the Torah's language, in which it is taking; later it uses *lishna de'Rabbanan*, the Sages' language.
Why do the Sages call it *kiddushin*? "*De'asar lah a'kula alma ke'hekdesh*": he forbids her to everyone, like consecrated property.
The comparison is incomplete: *hekdesh* is forbidden even to the one who consecrated it, and one can consecrate only what one already owns. Neither fits a husband.

Tosafot on "*harei at mekudeshet li*": the word "*li*" means she is forbidden to the world because she is bound to me, as things consecrated "to Heaven" are forbidden to all else. The exclusivity rests on a relationship, not on ownership.
*Hekdesh* too can be read as dedication rather than transfer of ownership, as when an animal is set apart as a *korban*; so *kiddushin* can be read as an exclusive dedication.

Two models of marriage run through the first chapter. The *kinyan* model: the man acquires something in her, perhaps sexual rights (the wife's duty is assumed, never derived) and the children (the Torah pays the husband for a miscarriage). The *kiddushin* model: a personal status of exclusivity created through a relationship.

Every Mishnah in the tractate speaks of *kiddushin* except this one. Its terse lists of objects and modes of *kinyan* reflect an early stratum; once the payment became a token and the *mohar* moved to the *ketubah*, the institution was renamed *kiddushin*.

chart.caption: Two ways of understanding marriage that the first chapter works through

A real price, like the Torah's *mohar*

sections.title: Ha'ishah Nikneit, Not Ha'ish Koneh: Ve'konah Et Atzmah or Mida'atah
sections.gist: Why the woman is the subject of the sentence: to match "she acquires herself", since "*koneh u'makneh*" fails when the husband dies; or to teach that *kiddushin* works only *mida'atah* (with her consent).

returns_to.note: Returns to the Mishnah's wording, now asking why the woman rather than the man is the subject

children.title: To Match Ve'konah Et Atzmah; Why Not 'Koneh U'makneh'
children.gist: The woman is the subject because the second clause, "she acquires herself", is about her; the man cannot be the subject throughout, since at his death it is Heaven that frees her.

bullets.text: Question: let this Mishnah too say "*ha'ish koneh*". Why make the woman the subject?
Answer: the latter clause says "*ve'konah et atzmah*", about her, so the first clause is also about her.
Question: then say "*ha'ish koneh u'makneh*", the man acquires and releases.
Answer: when the husband dies it is not he who releases her; her freedom comes *min ha'shamayim*, from Heaven.
Focusing on what is acquired is the chapter's pattern throughout: *ha'ishah nikneit*, *ha'yevamah nikneit*, then the *eved ivri*, the *eved kena'ani* and land.

children.title: Mida'atah: No Kiddushin Against Her Will
children.gist: A second answer: "*ha'ish koneh*" might imply he can act against her will, so the Mishnah says "*nikneit*" to require *mida'atah*.

bullets.text: Alternatively: had the Mishnah said "*ha'ish koneh*", one might think he can acquire her even against her will.
So it says "*ha'ishah nikneit*": *mida'atah*, yes; *she'lo mida'atah*, no.
In the Torah a father married off his daughter without asking her; only in Rivkah's story ("let us call the girl and ask her") is the bride consulted. Chazal limited the father's power to a minor.
The striking move: the one Mishnah that uses the language of *kinyan*, learned from buying a field, is read as insisting that the woman is a party to the act, not only its object.

sections.title: Shalosh or Sheloshah? Derekh as Feminine and as Masculine
sections.gist: Why the feminine "three": *derekh* (way) is feminine, yet a verse and the Mishnah on examining a *zav* (a man with a genital discharge) treat it as masculine; the Gemara reconciles both, then asks why the Mishnah said "ways" at all.

children.title: Derekh Is Feminine: 'Ha'derekh Yelkhu Vah'
children.gist: The Mishnah says *shalosh* rather than *sheloshah* because *derekh* is feminine, as a verse shows.

bullets.text: Question: why the feminine *shalosh* and not the masculine *sheloshah*?
Answer: the Mishnah wants to say *derekh*, which is feminine: "show them the way (*ha'derekh*) in which (*bah*) they must walk" (Shemot 18:20).

children.title: Contradictions Resolved: Torah vs. War, a Woman vs. the Zav
children.gist: A Mishnah on the *zav* and a verse on war treat *derekh* as masculine; the gender follows the subject: Torah and a woman are feminine, war and the *zav*'s examination are men's matters.

bullets.text: Challenge: the Mishnah in Nazir says "*be'shiv'ah derakhim* one examines a *zav*", using the masculine form. Why not the feminine *sheva*?
Answer: *derekh* is also masculine: "they shall come out against you *be'derekh echad* and flee before you *be'shiv'ah derakhim*" (Devarim 28:7).
Then the verses contradict each other, and so do the two *mishnayot*.
The verses: Shemot 18:20 speaks of the way of Torah, and Torah is feminine ("*Torat Hashem temimah*", Tehillim 19:8). Devarim 28:7 speaks of war, which is the way of a man and not of a woman.
The *mishnayot*: ours speaks of a woman, so it is feminine. The other speaks of examining a *zav*, which is done to a man.
A woman is not examined, since she is impure even from a discharge with an outside cause; a man is examined to see whether his discharge had another cause and is not *zivah*.
The examination asks whether the discharge came from food, sleep, an accident or another outside cause; only then does it matter.

children.title: 'Ways' or 'Matters'? Bi'ah Is Called a Derekh
children.gist: Why not say "three matters", in the masculine? Because the Mishnah wants to include *bi'ah*, which Scripture calls a *derekh*; the discussion continues.

bullets.text: Question: if *shalosh* is only because of *derekh*, let the Mishnah say "*devarim*" (matters), a masculine word, with *sheloshah*.
Answer: the Mishnah wants to teach *bi'ah*, and intercourse is called a *derekh*: "the way of a man with a young woman; so is the way of an adulterous woman" (Mishlei 30:19–20).

children.continues: Continues on 2b and 3a: why *kesef* and *shtar* also come under "ways", a second explanation from a baraita on a man pursuing a woman, other *mishnayot* that say "ways", and finally a general rule for "ways" versus "matters".

key_terms.sense: betrothal, the first stage of marriage
key_terms.definition: The act that makes a woman legally married to a man, forbidding her to all other men until a get or his death; it is made through kesef, shtar or bi'ah, before witnesses.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara explains the Sages' name for it: he forbids her to everyone like hekdesh, and contrasts it with the Torah's language of kinyan.

key_terms.definition: The second stage of marriage, at the chuppah, when the couple begin living together and the obligations of the household, such as the husband's support, take effect.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The shiur distinguishes it from kiddushin, and notes that the Torah's word kichah, from which kiddushin is learned, really describes nisu'in.

key_terms.definition: A formal act by which ownership or a legal right passes to a person, such as paying money, delivering a document or taking possession.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Only this Mishnah describes marriage with the language of kinyan, because it teaches kesef, learned from Avraham's acquisition of Efron's field.

key_terms.sense: money or value given as an act of kinyan or kiddushin
key_terms.definition: Giving money or an object of value as the act that effects an acquisition or a betrothal.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Beit Shammai require a dinar's worth and Beit Hillel a perutah's worth; it is learned from Efron's field by gezerah shavah.

key_terms.definition: A rule of interpretation that applies a law from one passage of Torah to another because the same word appears in both.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The word kichah (taking), used for a woman and for Efron's field, teaches that a woman is acquired with kesef.

key_terms.definition: Property dedicated to the Temple, removed from ordinary use and forbidden for personal benefit.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Sages call betrothal kiddushin because he forbids her to everyone as hekdesh is forbidden.

key_terms.definition: The requirement that a woman agree for kiddushin to take effect; kiddushin without her consent is void.
key_terms.on_this_daf: One answer for the wording ha'ishah nikneit is that it teaches kiddushin works mida'atah and not she'lo mida'atah.

judgment_calls: The two wording questions (nikneit vs. mekadesh, 2a.3–2b.2; nikneit vs. koneh, 2b.3–2b.5) could be one top-level section on the Mishnah's wording; kept apart because the first is about the vocabulary of kinyan and the second about who is the subject, with a returns_to link from the second.
The shiur's discussion of kichah in the Torah (nisu'in vs. erusin) and of Tosafot's questions has no Gemara lines of its own; kept as bullets in the Efron section rather than as separate sections.
The shiur's introduction to the tractate and its kinyan vs. kiddushin models were placed as bullets in the Mishnah section and the hekdesh section respectively, where they attach to the text.
The Mishnah's three ways and the kesef dispute both sit on line 2a.1; split into two children anchored to the same line, since they are distinct topics.
The 'ways or matters' question (2b.10) was kept under the shalosh section because it continues the same question of why the Mishnah says derakhim.
coverage_notes: Line 2b.10 (ways vs. matters) is not discussed in the shiur; outlined from the Gemara text only. The shiur's own material all falls within 2a.1–2b.9; none lies outside scope.

The essay presents the 'object-centered structure of the chapter' as the Gemara's answer for ha'ishah nikneit; the text answers only that the latter clause, ve'konah et atzmah, is about her. The structural point is marked as shiur.

The essay says the Italian issar was a copper coin; the Sefaria translation glosses it as a small silver coin (while calling the perutah copper). The outline keeps only the point that the perutah is copper and does not state the issar's metal.

The essay renders 'kach mimeni' as Efron saying 'take my money'; in the text (Bereshit 23:13) Avraham says 'I give the money for the field, take it from me'. Followed the text in stating Tosafot's point.
The essay attributes 'ki yikach ish isha u'va aleha' loosely; the Gemara's gezerah shavah cites Devarim 24:1. Followed the text.
